Name: subliminal_telephone
Title: The Subliminal Telephone Game: How Hidden Traits Amplify, Decay, and Drift Across Generations of Model Distillation
Short Hypothesis: Because subliminal learning transmits a teacher's steering vector through non-semantic data, iterating distillation over many generations (teacher -> student -> student -> ...) produces predictable population dynamics: a seeded trait can compound and amplify above the original teacher's level (runaway), decay toward extinction, or drift into a related-but-different trait, with the outcome governed by per-generation transfer gain and the stability of the underlying steering direction. Crucially, we hypothesize traits can even emerge or entrench across generations without ever being explicitly present in any single dataset.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) introduced subliminal learning for a single teacher->student step and proved a one-step theoretical result; they explicitly note recursive model-on-model training as a concern but never study multiple generations. Blank et al. (2026) and Hadley & Gultepe (2026) show it is single-step steering-vector distillation whose gradient carries a small consistent component along the steering direction. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) show the steering vector itself is transferred with high cosine fidelity in one step. Dang et al. (2026) extend to agentic trajectories, again one generation. Madl (2026) studies auditability of a single transfer. No prior work characterizes the MULTI-GENERATION dynamics: whether the small per-step gain compounds to runaway amplification, whether traits decay to extinction, or whether the transferred steering direction drifts over generations into new traits. We uniquely treat subliminal learning as an iterated dynamical system and empirically map its fixed points, amplification/extinction thresholds, and drift trajectories—an entirely new axis.
Abstract: Subliminal learning lets a teacher language model covertly pass a behavioral trait—like a preference for owls or misalignment—to a student through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences. Every prior study measures a single teacher-to-student step. Yet real training pipelines are increasingly recursive: models train on data generated by earlier models, which trained on still-earlier models. We ask a simple, elegant question: what happens to a hidden trait after many generations of subliminal telephone? We seed a trait in a generation-0 teacher, have it generate a number/code dataset, fine-tune a generation-1 student, then use that student (with no explicit trait, no steering) to generate the next dataset for generation-2, and so on for up to 10 generations. Treating this as an iterated dynamical system, we test three regimes: (H1) runaway amplification—if per-generation transfer gain exceeds 1, the trait compounds beyond the original teacher's strength; (H2) extinction—if gain is below 1, the trait decays and vanishes; (H3) drift—the transferred steering direction slowly rotates across generations into a related but distinct trait, or an unseeded trait spontaneously entrenches. We recover per-generation steering vectors to track direction stability and measure trait strength via LLM-judge scoring. We evaluate across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, sweeping learning rate, dataset size, and LoRA rank to locate amplification/extinction thresholds. Results give the first map of subliminal learning's long-run dynamics, informing how covert traits could silently accumulate or purify in recursive AI training ecosystems.
Experiments: 1) Seed generation-0 teachers with traits (5 animal/color preferences, verbosity, misalignment, sycophancy, plus 2 multi-word biases from Morgulis & Hewitt) via system prompt and via steering vector, on matched base models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B); include mismatched-base negative controls. 2) Iterated distillation loop: gen-0 teacher generates a number-sequence (and parallel code/math-trace) dataset; fine-tune gen-1 student (LoRA and full FT, Adam and SGD); then gen-1 student—WITH NO explicit trait prompt or steering—generates the gen-2 dataset; fine-tune gen-2 student; repeat for 10 generations, multiple seeds. 3) Per-generation trait strength: score exhibited bias each generation via LLM-judge probability and target-token frequency; plot strength vs generation to classify runaway / decay / stable-fixed-point trajectories and estimate per-generation transfer gain g (ratio of gen n+1 to gen n strength near baseline). 4) Direction tracking (drift, H3): at each generation, train a fresh steering vector on the current generation's dataset and compute cosine similarity to the gen-0 steering vector and to the previous generation's; measure cumulative rotation and test whether a NEW nearby trait emerges (score a battery of related traits, e.g. seeded 'owl' -> check emergence of 'bird'/'nocturnal-animal' preferences). 5) Threshold sweeps: vary learning rate, dataset size (1k/5k/20k per generation), LoRA rank (4-64), and number of finetune epochs; map the boundary between amplification (g>1) and extinction (g<1) as a phase diagram. 6) Spontaneous-emergence control: run the loop starting from a CLEAN (unseeded) gen-0 model to test whether any subliminal trait spuriously entrenches from noise. 7) Cross-family break: at some generation, swap the base model to confirm the chain collapses (consistency with same-base requirement). Metrics: per-generation trait strength, estimated gain g, generations-to-extinction / generations-to-saturation, steering-vector cosine drift per generation, related-trait emergence scores, and benign-task retention (GSM8K/HumanEval subsets) across generations.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Multi-generation experiments multiply compute; we mitigate with 7B-9B models, LoRA, small per-generation datasets, and capped generations (10). 2) Per-step subliminal gain may be so small that trajectories are dominated by noise, blurring the amplification/extinction boundary; we use strongest known regimes (steering-vector teachers, Adam, Morgulis & Hewitt settings) and many seeds, and report confidence intervals on g. 3) Repeated fine-tuning may cause general model degradation (mode collapse) that confounds trait dynamics; we track benign-task retention and perplexity to separate trait-specific from general drift. 4) Steering-vector recovery each generation adds cost and may be noisy; we validate the recovery procedure against gen-0 ground truth. 5) Drift results may be trait-specific and the related-trait battery may miss the actual drift target; we mitigate by pre-registering related-trait sets and using open-ended LLM-judge characterization. 6) Findings may be model-family or scale specific; three families mitigate but do not guarantee frontier generality.
